PP106: Democracy: Faltering demand in Africa?
text_paragraph_1: Democracy in Africa has faced considerable challenges over the past decade. According  to the Lexical Index of Electoral Democracy (Skaaning, 2021), while most of the democracies  surveyed by Afrobarometer a decade ago have maintained democratic rule, several have  experienced democratic backsliding in the years since to “multiparty autocracies” (Benin,  Nigeria, Côte d’Ivoire, Mozambique, Sierra Leone, and Tanzania) or military regimes (Burkina  Faso, Madagascar, and Mali). Only one country has improved its position, as Zambia  returned to “electoral democracy” status in 2021 (Herre, Rodés-Guirao, & Ortiz-Ospina,  2026a; France24, 2026). As measured by V-Dem’s (2026) indices of liberal democracy, many  other countries have experienced declines in the quality of electoral contestation and political freedoms over the same period (Herre, Rodés Guirao, & Ortiz-Ospina, 2026b).
text_paragraph_2: These developments raise the question: How hungry are ordinary Africans  for democracy?
text_paragraph_3: Since its inception, Afrobarometer’s surveys have contained sets of questions that measure the extent to which people want to live in a democratically governed society (or what we call “demand for democracy”) and the  degree to which they believe they are living in a democracy (what we have termed the  perceived “supply of democracy”).

For Liberia, Industrialization Will Be Measured in Megawatts
text_paragraph_1: Industrial policy can only succeed with both sustained political commitment and abundant, reliable energy. Liberia has the political will but needs to resolve its power question. A new injection of grant funds from the Millennium Challenge Corporation is an opportunity to link Liberia’s industrialization ambitions in rubber and iron ore with meaningful, timely, debt-free investments in Liberia’s power sector. The Government of Liberia should use this grant funding where it is most needed — transmission and utility reform — to leverage additional generation, whether through private investment or the West African Power Pool. This critical confluence can kickstart Liberia’s economic growth and job creation, if it can take advantage of the moment.
text_paragraph_2: To effectively execute on industrial policy, a country needs many things. This memo focuses on two of the most important: sustained political commitment and abundant, reliable energy. Liberia offers an instructive case study of when you have the will but lack the power.
text_paragraph_3: Over the past two administrations, Liberia has demonstrated an unusual degree of political continuity around industrial policy. Former President George Weah’s Executive Order 124 prohibited the export of unprocessed natural rubber. Current President Joseph Boakai subsequently extended the policy through Executive Order 151. Across party lines, the government has maintained a consistent objective: move Liberia away from raw commodity exports and toward domestic processing and value addition, starting with rubber (Liberia’s largest export crop). That consensus solves one of the most difficult problems in industrial development — political continuity and predictability. The next challenge is more practical: whether Liberia’s energy system can support the industrialization the nation seeks.

text_paragraph_1: Barrick, which operates in Tanzania in partnership with the government through Twiga Minerals, has supported residents of Kiseriani Village in Engikaret Ward, Longido District, and local leaders in completing the construction of classrooms and other school infrastructure at Shikinzi Primary School.
text_paragraph_2:
The project is aimed at addressing the challenge faced by pupils in the area who previously had to walk long distances to access education, exposing them to potential risks as they passed through areas inhabited by dangerous wild animals.
Speaking during the inauguration of the school in the village, Barrick Tanzania Resident Manager, Dr Melkiory Ngido, said the company's commitment to investing in education had prompted it to support efforts to address the challenges facing children in the area.
He said some children had been walking as far as 32 kilometres to and from school each day, making the construction of the school an important intervention.
“As Barrick, we are proud to be part of this journey to advance education in Tanzania. It is our commitment to continue working with the Government to ensure that Tanzanian children have access to education in better and more conducive learning environments,” Dr Ngido said.
He said Barrick would continue working with local communities to develop education infrastructure, noting that residents had demonstrated strong commitment and integrity in supporting the construction project.
The company contributed more than Sh180 million towards the construction of two classrooms and a teachers' office, helping to ensure that pupils could access quality education in a safe and conducive environment.
Dr Ngido commended residents of Kiseriani Village, many of whom are from the Maasai pastoralist community, together with their leaders, for their commitment to ensuring the successful completion of the school project.
He urged them to continue sending their children to school, saying education was an important tool for breaking the cycle of poverty and enabling young people to become self-reliant.
Speaking at the event, Longido Member of Parliament and Deputy Minister for Minerals, Dr Steven Kiruswa, thanked Barrick for supporting development projects that benefit communities across Tanzania, particularly in education, health, water and road infrastructure.
He said he would continue working with residents of the constituency to implement projects aimed at improving their livelihoods.
Dr Kiruswa pledged 100 bags of cement towards the construction of additional classrooms at the school. He also commended residents for contributing labour to the project, including transporting stones, sand and gravel.
Barrick is also implementing various education development projects through its Corporate Social Responsibility (CSR) programmes in communities surrounding its North Mara and Bulyanhulu mines.
In partnership with the Government, the company is implementing the Barrick-Twiga Future Forward Education Programme at a cost of more than Sh70 billion. The programme supports the construction of classrooms, dormitories and toilet facilities at secondary schools across Tanzania.
The programme, which has entered its second phase, aims to construct 1,090 classrooms, 1,640 sanitation and toilet facilities, and 270 dormitories at 161 schools across the country.
The initiative is intended to provide Tanzanian children with better learning and teaching environments for both pupils and teachers.
Since the formation of Twiga Minerals in 2020, Barrick has worked with the Government to develop Tanzania's mining sector and enhance its contribution to national productivity and sustainable development.

text_paragraph_1: On August 5, 2024, the Pentagon completed the handover of Air Base 201—a facility near Agadez, Niger, built at a cost of roughly $110 million and once billed as the largest U.S. Air Force-led construction project in the service’s history—to Niger’s military junta. The drawdown had begun on May 19 under mutually agreed withdrawal conditions; Air Base 101 in Niamey was turned over on July 7. On September 16 the Defense Department declared the withdrawal complete, including the departure of the AFRICOM Coordination Element and its two-star general. A presence that had peaked near 1,000 personnel was gone in under four months.
text_paragraph_2: What came next is instructive—and should be studied carefully rather than simplified. The narrative that Russia’s Africa Corps simply walked into U.S. bases and plugged in their equipment requires factual correction. What happened is more complicated, and in some ways more troubling.
text_paragraph_3: The Russian military—operating through the rebranded Wagner Group network now formally designated Africa Corps and reportedly overseen by Russian military intelligence (GRU)—had already established a presence in Niger before U.S. forces completed their withdrawal. Then-Defense Secretary Lloyd Austin confirmed in May 2024, and the BBC reported at the time, that Russian troops were moved into a wing of Air Base 101 near Niamey while American personnel were still present at the facility. That specific, documented overlap—Russian forces occupying one section of a base while U.S. forces occupied another—is a remarkable data point about the speed of the strategic transition.

text_paragraph_1: Babagana Ahmadu , the Representative of the United Nations (UN) Food and Agriculture Organisation (FAO) in Pretoria, recently died on a flight to Newark en route to Atlanta. Unlike many overcautious UN bureaucrats who unconsciously cut the figure of a “glorified nobody,” Babagana was a man of passion and ideas who also ran a farm in his volatile northeastern Nigerian hometown of Maiduguri. He was a practical man who literally liked to get his hands dirty. Before coming to South Africa in 2023, in an 18-year career, Babagana had been FAO Representative in Namibia, Gambia, and Sudan: fittingly for a dyed-in-the wool Pan-African, he had covered Southern, West, and Eastern Africa. In Addis Ababa – the capital of African diplomacy – he also worked as the first ever Director for Rural Economy and Agriculture in the African Union (AU) Commission under the leadership of former Malian president, Alpha Konaré (2003-2007). Babagana’s dedicated service to FAO in Gambia was acknowledged when he was awarded the Insignia of Commander of the National Order of the Republic on his departure in 2013, with the country’s leader, Yahya Jammeh, also praising his “unprecedented” achievements during his five-year tenure.
text_paragraph_2: Tirelessly traversing rural communities in Gambia, Babagana sought particularly to build infrastructure to support sustainable vegetation production; to increase the productive capacity of women farmers in vegetable farming and fish processing; and to improve storage facilities. In Sudan, he prioritised food security, climate change, and alleviating the deleterious impacts of internal conflicts, at a time, in 2022, when FAO was providing life-saving assistance to more than 2.5 million vulnerable Sudanese.
text_paragraph_3: His main concern was always the most vulnerable groups: women, children, herders, and rural farmers who struggled to acquire funding, technologies, markets, and agricultural inputs.

Earth From Orbit Is Unpredictable and Messy. Could 'Liquid' AI Clear the View?
text_paragraph_1: Monitoring Earth from above is a messy, inconsistent business. Clouds can block a satellite view, the angle of the Sun can create huge shadows, and orbital paths might not take a system across the same general area for weeks. That inconsistency is hard to deal with for traditional software, and can even confuse standard deep learning algorithms. But, according to a new review paper, available in pre-print by researchers Raul-Alexandru Gorgan and Dorian Gorgan of the Technical University of Cluj-Napoca, there’s a new type of frontier AI that could be able to help - bio-inspired Liquid Neural Networks.
text_paragraph_2: Modern society relies heavily on Earth observation, but collecting data in a meaningful way that is understandable to a deep learning system is complicated. For example, most deep learning networks, such as those that drive autonomous cars, expect data points to come in at regular intervals, and usually for those intervals to be relatively short, so that small changes can be distinguished and used to inform the model.
text_paragraph_3: That level of regularity doesn’t happen in Earth observation. The most obvious culprit is clouds. Satellites in Low Earth Orbit (LEO) can have their views of certain areas over the planet blocked by clouds - repeatedly in many cases. Combine that with relatively erratic flyover schedules, and some satellites can go over a month between being able to take pictures of certain parts of the world.

Having campaigned on a promise of transparency in the 2024 presidential elections, the government soon found itself facing an unexpectedly high level of debt.
text_paragraph_2: A report by the Court of Auditors revealed that between 2019 and 2024, the previous government led by President Macky Sall took on undisclosed loans worth 25 per cent of the country’s gross domestic product (GDP). At the end of 2024, public debt suddenly reached the equivalent of 132 per cent of GDP, triggering a downward spiral of poor financing conditions, a loss of confidence and political polarisation. The IMF subsequently froze its $1.8 billion programme in 2025. This put one of the new government’s key promises to the test: to reclaim Senegal’s economic and fiscal sovereignty. The current debt crisis shows just how limited the room for manoeuvre is for a country that remains dependent on international financing.
text_paragraph_3: The issue of how to deal with the debt burden is dividing the country. What was initially a technical problem turned into a political one, ultimately leading to a split within the governing PASTEF party, which has been in power since 2024. On 22 May 2026, Senegalese president Bassirou Diomaye Faye dismissed his prime minister and former mentor Ousmane Sonko. During the election campaign, the duo – who embodied the political change of 2024 – had emphasised national sovereignty through economic and fiscal independence. Sonko in particular repeatedly made it clear that debt restructuring would be tantamount to humiliation, thereby giving the impression that the country could break free from the existing structures and dependencies. Thus, PASTEF supporters claim on social media that, under Sonko, the party had raised almost 1.7 billion francs in just seven months — without IMF assistance.

title: PP106: Democracy: Faltering demand in Africa?
text_paragraph_1: Democracy in Africa has faced considerable challenges over the past decade. According  to the Lexical Index of Electoral Democracy (Skaaning, 2021), while most of the democracies  surveyed by Afrobarometer a decade ago have maintained democratic rule, several have  experienced democratic backsliding in the years since to “multiparty autocracies” (Benin,  Nigeria, Côte d’Ivoire, Mozambique, Sierra Leone, and Tanzania) or military regimes (Burkina  Faso, Madagascar, and Mali). Only one country has improved its position, as Zambia  returned to “electoral democracy” status in 2021 (Herre, Rodés-Guirao, & Ortiz-Ospina,  2026a; France24, 2026). As measured by V-Dem’s (2026) indices of liberal democracy, many  other countries have experienced declines in the quality of electoral contestation and political freedoms over the same period (Herre, Rodés Guirao, & Ortiz-Ospina, 2026b).
text_paragraph_2: These developments raise the question: How hungry are ordinary Africans  for democracy?
text_paragraph_3: Since its inception, Afrobarometer’s surveys have contained sets of questions that measure the extent to which people want to live in a democratically governed society (or what we call “demand for democracy”) and the  degree to which they believe they are living in a democracy (what we have termed the  perceived “supply of democracy”).

From MODH to HIRAAB: The Changing Face of Political Power in Somalia
text_paragraph_1: The political history of modern Somalia cannot be understood without examining the relationship between clan organization, pastoral society, and the construction of the modern state. In A Pastoral Democracy, published in 1961, I. M. Lewis described Somali pastoral society as a political order in which lineage, clan affiliation, contractual solidarity, and negotiated authority formed the foundations of political life. Lewis did not simply portray Somali society as a collection of competing tribes. Rather, he described a sophisticated system in which political obligations were distributed through kinship, alliances, and contractual relationships, while authority was constrained by the dispersed nature of power among lineage groups.
text_paragraph_2: The strength of this system was also one of its weaknesses when transferred into the politics of a modern state. Clan identity could provide security, social welfare, and mechanisms for resolving disputes where state institutions were weak. But when access to ministries, military commands, parliamentary seats, public employment, and economic resources became dependent upon control of the central government, lineage solidarity could be transformed into competition for state power.
text_paragraph_3: The creation of the Somali Republic in 1960 represented a decisive effort to replace localized political structures with a unified national order. Nationalism, Islam, and a shared Somali identity offered alternatives to narrow lineage loyalties. Yet the parliamentary era revealed the difficulty of building centralized governance within a decentralized society. Although political parties promoted national interests, regional, lineage, and clan loyalties continued to shape political competition, contributing to defections, factionalism, and succession disputes that weakened democratic stability.

Governor Gordon Joins Members of the Wyoming National Guard in Tunisia for International Security Exercise
text_paragraph_1: Governor Mark Gordon (R-WY) recently joined members of the Wyoming National Guard in Tunisia , where he participated in activities surrounding Exercise African Lion 2026, the largest annual joint military exercise led by the U.S. Africa Command. Held in Tunis, Tunisia, the exercise brought together military forces from the United States, Tunisia, and more than 40 partner nations to strengthen regional security cooperation and enhance readiness in an increasingly complex global environment.
text_paragraph_2: Governor Gordon said the more than two decade partnership between Wyoming and Tunisia stands as an example of the solidarity of nations which value freedom. Gordon added that he was also able to encourage the partnership between governments and academic institutions dealing with global issues such as agricultural strength, natural resource management, energy, and cybersecurity and computer technology.
text_paragraph_3: African Lion 2026 marks Tunisia’s tenth consecutive year as a host nation and represents the first phase of a broader multinational effort that will continue in Ghana, Morocco, and Senegal.  The exercise includes more than 5,600 personnel and highlights a Total Force approach, integrating active-duty military with National Guard, Reserve, Air Force, and Marine Corps units.
